subsection: 3. The annual Budget and workers; informed decisions as an employee

notes.b: Every year the government decides how much money to collect from people and businesses and how to spend it. That plan is the Budget, and it reaches workers through their pay, the services they use and the wider economy.
points: The government raises money mainly through taxes and spends it on services and social welfare (payments to people who are unemployed, retired, ill or caring for others). If spending is more than the money raised there is a deficit, and if it is less there is a surplus.

The annual Budget is the government's plan for raising tax and spending in the coming year. It is usually announced in the autumn for the following year, in October: Budget 2026 was announced on 7 October 2025 and Budget 2027 on 6 October 2026.

The Minister for Finance presents the Budget. Its tax changes are given legal effect through the Finance Act, a new Act each year, after debate in the Oireachtas (the Dáil and Seanad, which pass Ireland's laws).
The Budget sets tax bands, tax credits, social welfare rates and spending on services such as health, education and housing.
Workers are affected directly, through their take-home pay, and indirectly, through the quality and cost of the public services they use.
notes.tip: Keep the Budget and the Finance Act apart: the Budget is the announcement of the plan, and the Finance Act is the law that makes the tax changes happen. Say the Budget is usually announced in October rather than on a fixed day.

notes.h: Income tax, tax credits and bands
notes.b: Income tax is charged in bands and reduced by credits. Two ideas are easy to confuse: the band (how much income is taxed at one rate) and the credit (a sum taken off the tax owed).
points: Income tax is charged on taxable income at different rates across bands. Changing the width of a band changes how much tax a worker pays: widening the band taxed at the lower rate means less tax for those earning above the old threshold.
Tax credits reduce the tax a person owes, so an increase in a credit raises take-home pay for everyone who claims it by the same amount, whatever their income.

A tax band decides the rate at which income is taxed, while a tax credit is subtracted from the tax bill after it has been calculated. This is why a credit helps low and high earners equally, while a band change helps only those whose income reaches the band.

As announced in October 2026, Budget 2027 raises the standard-rate (40%) threshold for a single person from €44,000 to €46,500. It also raises the personal, PAYE and earned income tax credits by €125 each, with tax changes taking effect from January 2027.
notes.tip: A common mistake is to confuse credits with bands. If asked how a change alters net pay, name the measure, say whether it lowers the tax bill or the income taxed at the higher rate, and state the effect on take-home pay.

notes.b: Income tax is not the only charge on pay. The Universal Social Charge and PRSI are separate deductions, and a Budget can change them without touching income tax.
points: The Universal Social Charge (USC) is a separate charge on gross income (pay before deductions), with its own bands, paid in addition to income tax. It is a different charge from income tax and should not be treated as the same thing.
As announced in October 2026, Budget 2027 raises the upper limit of the 2% USC band by €1,600 to €30,300. This means more of a worker's income is charged at the lower rate.

PRSI (Pay Related Social Insurance) is a contribution from pay that funds certain social welfare benefits, such as illness benefit and the State pension, and builds the worker's insurance record, which affects entitlement to those benefits.

A Budget change to income tax, tax credits or USC can alter net pay (pay after deductions) even when gross pay stays the same. For example, a larger tax credit leaves a worker with more take-home pay without any pay rise.
notes.tip: Treat income tax, USC and PRSI as three separate things. Do not confuse PRSI, which builds a record for benefits, with pension savings, and do not quote rates from memory.

notes.h: Minimum wage, social welfare and other supports
notes.b: Budgets also change the wages and supports that sit alongside tax. Each measure helps some groups, and each has a cost for someone else.
points: Minimum wage decisions raise the income of low-paid workers, but they also add to employers' costs, which can affect hiring.
As of 2026 the adult rate is €14.15 an hour from 1 January 2026. Budget 2027 announced a rise of 79 cent to €14.94 an hour from 1 January 2027.
Social welfare changes affect households with children, jobseekers, carers and pensioners, and some payments are means tested (given only to people whose income falls below a set level).
Budget 2027 raises weekly social welfare rates by €10 from January, raises the fuel allowance by €5 to €43 a week and raises the home carer credit by €100.

Childcare supports lower the cost of early education and care, which makes it easier for parents to take up or keep work. Budget 2027 cuts the maximum creche fee from €735 to €550 for children up to senior infants from September 2027.

Housing supports, including social housing and help with rent, change how much of a worker's income is left after housing costs. Budget 2027 raises the rent tax credit by €150 to €1,150 for a single renter.
Cost-of-living measures, such as one-off payments or credits, boost income for a period without changing the tax system, so they do not permanently change a worker's tax position.
notes.tip: When you outline what a measure means for a worker, name the group affected, such as low-paid workers, parents or renters.

notes.b: Not every tax comes out of pay. Indirect taxes are added to the price of what people buy, so a Budget can change a worker's spending power without touching their payslip.
points: Indirect taxes (taxes added to the price of goods, such as VAT and excise duties) affect consumers' spending power even when income taxes are unchanged.
Budget 2027 postponed the restoration of petrol and diesel excise from 1 November to 28 February, with restoration then in stages. The postponement is not the end of the change.
notes.tip: Give figures only with their date, as announced in October 2026.

notes.b: Many workers currently have no pension. Auto-enrolment is the State's response: workers are signed up by default, so saving for retirement becomes the normal choice rather than something they must set up themselves.
points: Auto-enrolment is a system in which eligible workers are enrolled in a workplace pension by default, with the option to opt out. Starting costs the worker no effort, which is why more people end up saving.

Contributions come from the worker, the employer and the State, which is intended to increase retirement savings. MyFutureFund, the State system, began collecting contributions on 1 January 2026, and it is run by the National Automatic Enrolment Retirement Savings Authority (NAERSA).
In 2026 to 2028 the employee and the employer each pay 1.5% of gross pay and the State adds 0.5%, and the rates rise in stages over ten years. The State adds €1 for every €3 the employee pays.
Many workers have no pension, and saving early benefits from long-term growth on the money invested, because contributions made in the early years have longer to grow.

Before opting out, a worker should check the contribution rate, the employer's contribution and the State top-up, because opting out gives up the employer's and State's money as well as the worker's own.
notes.tip: Explain what to check rather than telling a worker what to do: do not write 'you should opt out'. Pension enrolment and contributions are managed through an online portal, so employees should check their details and records online.

notes.h: Trade-offs and who gains from a Budget
notes.b: No Budget can please everyone, because the government has a limited amount of money. Every measure helps one group and costs something elsewhere, and a good answer shows both sides.
points: A Budget is a trade-off: tax cuts can reduce the money available for public services, while higher spending may require higher taxes or borrowing.

Low-paid workers may gain most from minimum wage increases and targeted credits, while higher earners may be more affected by changes to tax bands. A higher minimum wage, however, adds to employers' costs.

A tax credit raises take-home pay by the same amount for everyone who claims it, while a band change helps only those whose income reaches the band. This is why the two measures can be judged differently for fairness.

Fairness is an ethical question: a measure that gives one group a large gain and another group little raises the question of whether the Budget is fair. Claims about the 'average' gain can hide how different groups are affected, so read them honestly.
Budget decisions on fuel excise and carbon-related taxes balance cost-of-living relief against environmental goals. Long-term pension saving is also a form of financial sustainability for workers.
notes.tip: A common mistake is to give only gains and no trade-offs. A full answer names the measure, says how it changes net pay, names the groups affected and gives one trade-off, such as the cost to the Exchequer (the government's central funds) or the effect on employers.

notes.b: A payslip shows how gross pay becomes the money that lands in the bank. Reading it lets a worker see exactly where Budget changes show up.
points: Gross pay is pay before any tax or other deductions are taken out.
Deductions include income tax, USC, employee PRSI, and any pension or union contributions the worker has agreed to pay.
Net pay, also called take-home pay, is gross pay less all deductions.

A sample worker on a sample gross wage shows the layout: gross pay at the top, then income tax, USC, PRSI and pension as deductions, then net pay at the bottom. The figures are for illustration only, not real rates.
Checking the payslip against the hours worked and the agreed rate helps a worker spot errors early, because a mistake in hours or rate flows into every deduction.
Payslips and tax records are digital, so employees should check them online.
notes.tip: Never say a tax cut raises gross pay: it changes deductions and so raises net pay. Keep gross and net pay separate.

notes.b: An informed employee looks beyond the headline wage. Good decisions about a job depend on the whole package and on how government decisions change take-home pay.
points: An informed employee checks the contract, understands pension options and knows their statutory rights (rights set by law) before making decisions.

Comparing jobs should include benefits such as pension matching (a sample business matching the employee's pension contribution), sick pay and flexible working, not only the headline pay, because a lower wage with strong benefits can be worth more overall.
Understanding how Budget changes affect take-home pay helps workers plan their saving and spending.
Employees on the margins, such as gig workers, may have a different tax and pension position from other workers.
notes.tip: Compare jobs on total benefits, not headline pay. State what a worker should check, not what they should decide.

notes.b: Workplace and Budget stories give a chance to apply everything above. The skill is to analyse a story rather than copy its headline.
points: Workplace news often covers pay disputes, redundancies, Budget measures and new employment rights, and each needs a clear view of who gains and who loses.
Reading workplace news critically means identifying the decision, who is affected and the evidence behind the claims made.
Analyse a story by identifying the decision, its effect on workers, the government's reasons and the trade-offs involved.

Example 1, Budget 2027 (October 2026, Irish Times, 6 October 2026): the decision is a package of tax and welfare changes, with effects of higher take-home pay for earners, renters and parents. The trade-off is the cost to the Exchequer.

Example 2, the start of MyFutureFund auto-enrolment (January 2026, gov.ie): the decision is a State retirement savings system, with workers saving more for retirement. The trade-offs are less take-home pay now and extra cost for employers.
notes.tip: A headline may be given as stimulus. Identify the decision, the effect on workers, the government's reason and a balanced judgement with evidence from the story, and do not copy the headline without analysis.

keyTerms.definition: The government's yearly plan for raising tax and spending for the coming year.
Ranges of income taxed at different rates, such as the standard rate band and the higher rate band.
An amount deducted from the tax a person owes, reducing their tax bill.
A separate charge on gross income, with its own bands, paid in addition to income tax.
Pay Related Social Insurance, a contribution from pay that funds certain social welfare benefits and the State pension.
Pay before any tax or other deductions are taken out.
Pay left after all deductions, also called take-home pay.
A system where eligible workers are automatically signed up to a pension scheme, with the option to opt out.
A temporary or targeted payment or credit from the State to offset rising living costs.

factCards.term: Effect of a credit on take-home pay
factCards.definition: It reduces the tax owed, so take-home pay rises without any change in gross pay.

questions.prompt: Explain how the annual Budget can affect workers, using at least three measures in your answer.
questions.model: The Budget changes tax bands and tax credits, which alter the amount of income tax a worker pays and so their take-home pay. Changes to USC and PRSI rates or bands have a similar effect, and PRSI also affects entitlement to benefits such as the State pension. Minimum wage decisions raise the hourly pay of the lowest-paid workers, but they add to employers' costs. Childcare and housing supports change how much of a worker's income is left after essential costs. Each measure is a trade-off, because a tax cut can reduce the funds available for public services.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between gross pay and net pay, and outline two deductions that reduce gross pay.
questions.model: Gross pay is the amount earned before any tax or other deductions are taken out, while net pay, or take-home pay, is what remains after all deductions. Two deductions are income tax, which is charged on taxable income across bands, and employee PRSI, which funds social welfare benefits and affects entitlement to them. USC and any agreed pension contribution are further deductions.

questions.prompt: Outline the purpose of auto-enrolment pensions and explain one reason a worker might still choose to opt out.
questions.model: Auto-enrolment aims to increase retirement saving by signing eligible workers up to a workplace pension by default, with contributions from the worker, the employer and the State. A worker might opt out if they need the extra take-home pay immediately, for example because they face urgent debts, although opting out means losing the contributions from the employer and the State.
